title: Sony FE 600mm f/6.3 GM OSS duyuruldu
summary: Sony, elde taşımayı kolaylaştıran hafif yapısıyla dikkat çeken yeni süper telefoto lensi Sony FE 600mm f/6.3 GM OSS modelini tanıttı.
body:
Fstoppers'ın aktardığına göre, kuş ve yaban hayatı fotoğrafçıları için geliştirilen Sony FE 600mm f/6.3 GM OSS duyuruldu. Yaklaşık 1 kilogram ağırlığındaki yeni lens, fotoğrafçılara gün boyu elde çekim yapma imkânı sunarak ağır modellerin yarattığı kol yorgunluğunu ortadan kaldırmayı hedefliyor. Profesyonel fotoğrafçı Jan Wegener'in yeni lensle gerçekleştirdiği ilk testlerde, özellikle hızlı hareket eden kuş çekimlerinde başarılı sonuçlar elde edildiği belirtildi.

## Hafif gövde ve performans

Fstoppers'ın paylaştığı bilgilere göre, Sony'nin yeni lensi 3.698 dolar fiyat etiketiyle satışa sunuluyor. Yaklaşık 3 kilo ağırlığındaki Sony FE 600mm f/4 GM OSS modeline kıyasla üçte bir oranında hafif olan bu lens, gün boyu süren çekimlerde büyük bir ergonomik avantaj sağlıyor. Wegener, testler sırasında lense Sony FE 1.4x ve 2x telekonverter ekleyerek odak mesafesini sırasıyla 840mm ve 1200mm'ye çıkardığını, ancak daha yüksek odaklarda diyaframın düşmesiyle birlikte otomatik odaklamanın biraz zorlaştığını aktardı. Ayrıca lensin elde çekilen video çekimlerinde bazı sabitleme sorunları yaşatabildiği de gözlemlenen detaylar arasında yer aldı.

## Pazardaki yeri

Sony, bu modelle birlikte hafif ve yavaş diyaframlı uzun odaklı lens trendine katılmış oldu. Daha önce Nikon ve Canon da benzer hafif telefoto lens modellerini piyasaya sürmüştü. Günümüz dijital sensörlerinin yüksek ISO hassasiyeti ve gelişmiş nesne algılama özellikli otomatik odaklama sistemleri, fotoğrafçıların daha dar diyafram açıklıklarıyla çalışabilmesine olanak tanıyor.

**Neden önemli?** Yaban hayatı fotoğrafçılığında ekipman ağırlığı, sahada kalınan süreyi ve yakalanan kare sayısını doğrudan etkiliyor. Bu tür hafif lensler, fotoğrafçıların ağır ekipmanlar yüzünden kaçırdığı anları yakalayabilmesi açısından yeni bir alternatif sunuyor.

source_texts.text:
A 600mm prime that weighs about 1 kg and costs $3,698 reads like a list of compromises, and Sony's new 600mm f/6.3 asks you to give up aperture in exchange for a lens you can carry without a second thought. If you shoot birds or wildlife handheld, the gap between a lens you can hold for five minutes and one you can hold all morning decides how many chances you actually get.
After more than 20 years photographing birds professionally, Jan Wegener took the Sony FE 600mm f/6.3 GM OSS out with the Sony a1 II and came back with more keepers than he gets from lenses twice its size. His first test was rainbow bee-eaters, which are small, quick, and change direction constantly. Working close to the ground as the birds flew to and from their nest, he relied on the camera's 30 fps burst and pre-capture to catch sudden takeoffs. The lens weighs less than half as much as the Sony FE 200-600mm f/5.6-6.3 G OSS, and about a third as much as the roughly 3 kg Sony FE 600mm f/4 GM OSS. Wegener's arms tire fast with the big f/4, while the smaller lens let him keep tracking for hours. The bird that finally does something interesting tends to do it long after a heavy lens has worn you out.
For perched bee-eaters, Wegener added the Sony FE 1.4x Teleconverter, which turns the lens into an 840mm f/9. Sharpness and detail held up well with the converter attached, provided there was enough light for a quick shutter speed. Flight shots were harder. At f/9, holding 1/4,000 s gets tough, and he saw autofocus become less consistent than with the bare lens, though he still got usable frames. He then pushed further with the Sony FE 2x Teleconverter, reaching 1200mm at f/13. Minimum focus stays at 2.5 m, or a bit over 8 ft, so magnification climbs from about 0.25x to nearly 0.5x.
Sony is joining a direction other makers have been moving in for years. Nikon's AF-S 500mm f/5.6E PF ED VR arrived in 2018 at under 1.5 kg. Canon followed with the RF 600mm f/11 IS STM and RF 800mm f/11 IS STM in 2020, and Nikon later added the Z 800mm f/6.3 VR S and Z 600mm f/6.3 VR S. Two things made slower long glass workable. Modern sensors now produce clean files at ISO settings that used to be off-limits, and subject-detection autofocus locks onto birds without the extra light a fast aperture once supplied. If you're weighing a lens like this, open your last few hundred bird shots and check the aperture in the metadata. Many close-range bird images get stopped down to f/8 anyway for enough depth of field across the head and body, and in those frames the f/4's extra light was never used. Morning and evening light, dense cover, and anything you plan to shoot at high shutter speeds in shade are where a faster lens still earns its weight.
Wegener also took the bare lens into dark mangroves for tiny fairy-wrens, shooting at f/6.3 with an extra-large tracking spot so focus grabbed the bird the moment it landed on a perch. At a local lake, he worked his way close to a normally shy great crested grebe with a simple approach that you can use on other diving birds. He also ran into one issue that gave him real pause about buying the lens. The stabilization on the lens and camera combination looked shaky enough in handheld video to make the footage hard to use. He found a way around it while filming red-capped plover chicks barely 5 cm tall on a beach, and the method is easy to copy.
Watch the video above to see how Wegener got within range of that grebe and how his handheld plover footage turned out.
